title: Design: parking lot
objective: Go from requirements to classes for a parking lot: who holds which data, how a car is parked, how fees are worked out, and what breaks with two gates.

sources.title: Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides, Design Patterns (Addison-Wesley, 1994): the Strategy pattern (fee policies)
Python docs: threading Lock objects (one thread at a time)

simplifies: One lot in one process. A real system keeps spots in a database, where a transaction (not a Python lock) makes taking a spot atomic across many gates. Rates (₹40 an hour) are illustrative.

steps.caption: Requirements first: cars, bikes and trucks; small, medium and large spots on several floors; a ticket at entry; pay by time at exit. The nouns are candidate classes.
Give each job to the class that has the data. Floor knows its spots, so Floor finds a free one.

predict.prompt: Who should decide whether a bike fits a spot?

options.text: Spot, with fits(vehicle): it knows its own size
options.explanation: Right. The rule lives next to the data it needs.

options.text: ParkingLot, by checking every spot's size itself
options.explanation: Then ParkingLot needs to know every spot type's rules.
The system has to check; drivers don't always choose well.

steps.caption: Parking a car: the lot asks a floor for a free spot…
…the floor asks each spot whether the car fits…
…and the lot writes a ticket for the spot it got.
Fees vary (hourly in malls, flat at events), so the ticket asks a FeePolicy: the Strategy pattern again.

predict.prompt: A car stays 2 hours 10 minutes at ₹40 an hour, rounded up. What's the fee?

options.explanation: Right. ceil rounds 2.17 hours up to 3, and 3 × 40 = 120.
That rounds down to 2 hours; ceil rounds up.
That charges for exact minutes; this policy rounds up to whole hours.

steps.caption: Two gates ask for a free spot at the same moment. If both read "B12 is free" before either marks it taken, both cars get B12. Taking a spot must happen one at a time (a lock here; a database transaction in real systems).

predict.prompt: Two entry gates call free_spot() at the same instant. What can go wrong?

options.text: Both get the same spot, unless finding and taking it happen as one step
options.explanation: Right. Check-then-act races are a classic concurrency bug.

options.text: Nothing: computers do one thing at a time
options.explanation: Two gates are two threads (or two servers); their steps can interleave.

options.text: The lot runs out of spots
options.explanation: There are spots; the problem is two cars getting the same one.

exercise.change: Add electric-vehicle spots that charge by the hour.
exercise.hint: Spot just stores a kind string. Which classes have an if/elif on spot.kind?

options.text: Let each spot type decide fits() and its own fee policy, so callers never branch on the kind; Floor creates the spots
options.explanation: Right. An EV spot is a new Spot subclass, plus one change where spots are built.

options.text: Add an 'ev' branch to each if-chain
options.explanation: That's three edits now, and three more for the next spot type.

options.text: Make a second ParkingLot just for EV spots
options.explanation: That copies the whole lot's logic and splits one car park in two.

exercise.explain: Spot types carry their own rules (fits, fee policy), so ParkingLot, Ticket and Board never mention kinds. Adding EV spots is a new EvSpot class, plus one change to Floor, which builds the spots.

quiz.prompt: In a design interview, what do you do first for "design a parking lot"?

options.text: Ask about requirements: vehicle types, spot sizes, payment, how many gates
options.explanation: Right. Classes come from requirements; guessing them wastes the interview.
Without requirements you don't know what Spot needs.
Storage comes after you know the objects and how they behave.

quiz.prompt: Why give Spot a fits(vehicle) method instead of checking sizes in ParkingLot?

options.text: Spot has the size data, so the rule lives next to it, and new spot types bring their own rule
options.explanation: Right. Callers ask; they don't need to know the rules.

options.text: ParkingLot can't read a spot's size
options.explanation: It could; the point is where the rule belongs.
